The "not a simulator" framing is misleading in a systematic review that is presumably distinguishing simulated from operational evidence. The honest classification is: dataset-replay benchmark on a public synthetic-testbed corpus, with throughput measured on the authors' own system. Additionally, CICIDS2017 has well-documented labelling errors in the subsequent literature (Engelen, Rimmer & Joosen 2021; Lanvin et al. 2022), which directly caps how much weight a 99.98% precision figure derived from it can carry.

(2) Scoping strip on the carried numbers. The source says "selected attacks in CICIDS 2017 dataset." The appraiser's carried strings drop that. If these numbers enter the manuscript they MUST carry the qualifier, e.g. "99.98% average precision / 93.42% average recall on selected attack classes in CICIDS2017 (Loganathan et al., GLOBECOM 2018)", and the throughput as ">2.5M events/sec on the authors' testbed (hardware not stated in the abstract; full text not accessible to this verifier)."

RESIDUAL UNCERTAINTY I am stating rather than papering over: I verified the numbers from the publisher-sourced abstract, not from the full text. I could not access the PDF. If the review intends to lean on these figures as anything more than an author-reported headline, someone with Xplore access should read the results tables and confirm (a) which attack classes were selected, (b) whether the CEP rule was tuned and evaluated on the same data, and (c) the hardware behind the 2.5M events/sec. The tuning-on-test risk is a live concern for a 99.98% precision claim and I could not rule it out.

RECOMMENDATION: CITE_WITH_CAVEAT — cite it, but demote the method basis from "real_measurement (real dataset, not a simulator)" to "author-reported benchmark on a synthetic public corpus with known label noise," and never carry the precision/recall numbers without the "selected attacks" scoping.

CONFIRMED VERBATIM (Conclusion, sec. 6): "Our evaluation shows a detection accuracy of >90%, and up to a 4,242x latency improvement on CPU and up to 18,000x improvement on a hardware accelerator. Also, our method consumes up to 5,300x and 12 orders of magnitude less energy than baseline with CPU and PIM accelerator, respectively." Abstract also carries ">90% detection accuracy and up to 4,242x speedups over the state-of-the-art."

1. ">90% detection accuracy" is NOT accuracy. Table 1 is titled "ROC-AUC scores for each TTP and hop length"; the averages are 0.934 / 0.898 / 0.912 / 0.913 across hop-lengths 0-3. Sec 5.2.2 says "our results have an average accuracy >90% across all TTPs and hop lengths" — but the underlying measured quantity is average ROC-AUC, and one of the four hop-length averages (0.898 at hop 1) is BELOW 0.90. No precision/recall/FPR is reported at all. Carrying ">90% detection accuracy" into a systematic review would propagate the paper's own metric mislabel.
2. The 18,000x and the "12 orders of magnitude" are SIMULATED, not measured. Sec 5.1.2 ("Simulation"): "We use NeuroSim to model a FeFET memory with 32 clusters... We use the latency and energy consumption of various in-memory operations from NeuroSim in our in-house cycle-based simulation to evaluate the behaviors of the PIM accelerator." 4. "5,300x less POWER" should be ENERGY (Joules). Fig 6 is "ECDF of energy consumption"; sec 5.2.1 says "our CPU results show 14 to 5,300x lower energy consumption". The intro sloppily says "power", the results and conclusion say energy. Also note 4,242x and 5,300x are the TOP of ranges (14-4,242x latency, 14-5,300x energy) and are the 15-TTP amortized case, not per-query.

TWO IMPORTANT CORRECTIONS to the appraiser's framing:
(1) The paper itself calls this an "experimental deployment" — "We did not encounter any significant performance issues ... during the experimental deployment with the presented configuration" (§4.2). So it is a real deployment ON a production sharing platform carrying real peer alerts, but the authors do not claim a hardened production service. The manuscript must not upgrade their own hedge.
(2) The appraiser was right that no precision/recall figures could be pulled — because the paper does not report any. §4 is explicitly observational ("we provide observations and comment on experiences gained"). Any accuracy figure attributed to AIDA would have to come from the companion papers (refs [14,15], Husák et al.), not this one.
records.verify_notes:
VENUE CHECK — PASSES, independently. The DOI 10.1145/3339252.3340513 resolves (302) from doi.org to dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3339252.3340513, so it is a real, publisher-assigned ACM DOI, not a Zenodo/self-deposit DOI and not a preprint server. The ACM DL landing page itself 403s to WebFetch (standard ACM bot-blocking, not an absence of record), but the DOI resolution plus the ACM Reference Format and ACM copyright/licensing lines printed inside the paper's own PDF independently establish ACM as publisher of record. ARES is a long-running (since 2006) security/dependability conference with ACM ICPS proceedings, DBLP/Scopus-indexed; it is not on any predatory list, has not been delisted, and the publisher (ACM) has no integrity/paper-mill issue. Authors are Martin Husák and Jaroslav Kašpar, Institute of Computer Science, Masaryk University, Brno (husakm@ics.muni.cz, kaspar@ics.muni.cz) — identifiable, institutional, with an open-source artifact (github.com/CSIRT-MU/AIDA-Framework) and a multi-year trail on the same SABU/Warden lineage. No integrity flags. The only refinement is workshop-vs-main-track (see venue_correction).

NUMBERS CHECK — PASSES for the claim actually being carried. The deployment claim is in the source, near-verbatim, and the scale (1.7M alerts/day, real peer-contributed IDS/honeypot alerts on CESNET's SABU) is confirmed. I got the PDF the appraiser could not get, so this is a first-hand read, not an inference from an abstract.

WHY CAVEAT RATHER THAN CLEAN CITE:
- The paper's own word for it is "experimental deployment" on a dedicated commodity server (Xeon E5520, 16 GB RAM) inside SABU. "Live analytical component of a production platform" is defensible — the alert stream is production — but the manuscript should say "deployed experimentally as an analytical component of the SABU alert-sharing platform, processing ~1.7M real IDS/honeypot alerts per day", not "production-hardened".
- The "method basis: real_measurement" label is only half right. The DATA are real (not simulated), which is the useful and genuinely rare property here, but the EVALUATION is observational/qualitative — the authors report operating experience and data-characterization percentages, not a controlled experiment with reported precision/recall. If the review's evidence table has a column for reported detection/prediction accuracy, AIDA's cell must be "not reported", not a number. Downgrading the method-basis label to something like "real-data operational deployment, observational evaluation" would be more honest than "real_measurement", which invites a reader to expect an accuracy figure that does not exist.
- Tier A is acceptable for the peer-review dimension (ACM, peer-reviewed proceedings), but if the review's tiering also encodes methodological strength, an 8-page workshop paper with no reported accuracy metrics is not the same evidentiary weight as a main-track paper with a controlled evaluation. Consider tier A for provenance with an explicit method-strength note, or B if the tier is a blended judgement.

BOTTOM LINE: cite it — for its architecture, its venue, and the real-alert-stream deployment on SABU (1.7M alerts/day), all of which I confirmed in the primary source. Do not attach any precision, recall, F1, or accuracy figure to this reference; the paper contains none, and the 0.5/0.6–0.9 values in it are rule support/confidence, which is a different quantity and would be exactly the kind of number-detached-from-source failure this repository has already been burned by.
